issues.description: The manuscript presents hypothesis tests, effect sizes, and substantive conclusions based on randomized placeholder data rather than observed participant responses. Statistical inference from simulated dummy data is not meaningful and cannot be treated as empirical evidence for or against any hypothesis.
issues.quote: "We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect."

issues.description: The manuscript gives inconsistent accounts of study status: it states that data collection was launched/completed, but also explicitly says the methods/results use randomized placeholder data to be replaced later. This makes it impossible to know whether the reported analyses are preregistration mock-ups or actual study results.
issues.quote: "Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period." / "[IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]" / "data collection was completed before analyses."

issues.description: Allowing participants to choose their condition eliminates random assignment and introduces selection confounds. Any observed differences could reflect pre-existing differences among participants who selected different conditions rather than the manipulation.
issues.quote: "Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions."

issues.description: The design is described as within-subject, but the reported analyses and cell counts are consistent with a between-subjects factorial design. In a true within-subject design, each participant would contribute data to multiple cells; here, the per-cell sample sizes sum to the total N, implying one cell per participant.
issues.quote: "We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively."

issues.description: If the design was truly within-subject as stated, a standard two-way ANOVA treating observations as independent is inappropriate; a repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed model would be required. If it was actually between-subjects, then the methods section is incorrect. Either way, the analytic model and design description do not align.
issues.quote: "We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation."

issues.description: The replication substantially alters the original studies by merging Study 1 and Study 3 into a new single experiment and by applying the explicit intervention to the joint condition. This changes the factorial structure and creates a new study rather than a close/direct replication of either original experiment.
issues.quote: "In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition..."

issues.description: The original study used real money donations with financial consequences; the replication replaces this with an imaginary donation response. Hypothetical willingness-to-donate is not equivalent to actual donation behavior and may engage different motivations and effect sizes.
issues.quote: "Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter."

issues.description: The replication changes the victim materials to updated information from Save the Children. Because identifiability effects are highly sensitive to vividness, emotional salience, and narrative details, changing the stimulus content may materially change the construct being manipulated.
issues.quote: "Updated victim information We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago."

issues.description: The manuscript classifies the study as a "close to very close replication" despite acknowledging different DV stimuli, different physical setting, different contextual variables, and different procedures. Those deviations are substantial enough that direct comparability to the original findings is weakened.
issues.quote: "DV stimuli | Different" / "Physical settings | Different | Online survey" / "Contextual variables | Different | MTurk workers as participants" / "Replication classification | close to very close replication"

issues.description: The manuscript states that the study was powered based on the original effects but does not report the key inputs (target power, alpha, assumed effect size, allocation, resulting required N) in the main text. Without these details, readers cannot evaluate whether the design was actually adequately powered.
issues.quote: "The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of 'Power analysis of the original study effect'."

issues.description: Exclusion criteria are mentioned, but the number excluded, reasons by category, and condition-wise losses are not reported. This is especially problematic because the reported cell sizes still sum to 1000 exactly, making it unclear whether exclusions were actually applied.
issues.quote: "Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check."

issues.description: Key recruitment details needed to assess sample comparability are missing, including compensation for the replication sample and even basic sample descriptors in the comparison table. This limits evaluation of motivational differences relative to the original donation study.
issues.quote: "Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified"

issues.description: The study assumes that reading about the identifiable victim effect or seeing statistics induces deliberative/analytical thinking, but no manipulation check is reported to verify that the intended cognitive process changed. Without evidence that deliberation was induced, null or positive findings are hard to interpret.
issues.quote: "The victim statistics was believed to eliminate the identifiable victim effect implicitly in the joint condition as reflected in the donation towards the identifiable victim."

issues.description: The manuscript reframes the joint presentation of identifiable and statistical information as "implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect." Exposure to statistics is not the same construct as learning a bias or engaging in explicit deliberation, so the theoretical interpretation of Hypothesis 4 is conceptually muddled.
issues.quote: "For Hypothesis 3 and 4, explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect means that participants would be presented with prior research about the phenomenon while participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition."

issues.description: The manuscript creates an "aggregated feelings" score by combining conceptually heterogeneous items (e.g., being upset, being touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and in places perceived impact). No reliability coefficient, factor analysis, or justification is provided to show these items form a coherent scale.
issues.quote: "Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling" / "Note: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)"

issues.description: Perceived impact of donation is an efficacy/evaluation judgment, not an affective reaction. Treating it as one of the "segregated affective reactions" blurs the theoretical mechanism under test and makes the aggregated-feelings construct less interpretable.
issues.quote: "We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions..." / "Perceived impact (Extension)"

issues.description: The manuscript uses correlational analyses to speak of affective feelings "predicting" donation and earlier frames this as examining the "effect" of affective feelings. Correlation across condition-specific subsets cannot establish that feelings causally influence donation, especially when both may be jointly driven by the manipulated context.
issues.quote: "We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation."

issues.description: The manuscript tests many outcomes separately (multiple feelings, three effects each, plus multiple subgroup correlations) but does not report a correction across this family of tests. The lone significant extension effect at p = .045 is particularly vulnerable to false-positive inflation under this level of multiplicity.
issues.quote: "Note: Segregated feelings include being upsetting, being touched, being sympathetic, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and perceived impact of donation (extension)" / "Perceived impact (Extension) | 2 | 3.11 | .006 | [0.00,0.02] | .045*"

issues.description: The reported post-hoc result is internally inconsistent: the Bonferroni-adjusted p-value is significant, but the 95% CI for d includes zero; additionally, the t statistic is negative while the reported d is positive. This suggests either the confidence interval, effect-size calculation, or sign coding is wrong.

The narrative interpretation of the donation results reverses the group labels relative to Table 7. Table 7 shows higher mean donations for the identifiable than the statistical condition when averaged across intervention levels, but the text states the opposite and assigns the means to the wrong groups.
issues.quote: "participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67)."

issues.description: The perceived-impact post-hoc comparison also shows a significant p-value with a 95% CI that includes zero, indicating inconsistent reporting. This makes the claimed extension result statistically unreliable as presented.

The abstract says the extension hypothesis was supported for lower perceived impact in identifiable/joint conditions, but Hypothesis 6 predicts the opposite direction (identifiable higher than statistical), and the reported pairwise results only show a statistical-vs-joint difference. The abstract therefore overstates and misstates the extension finding.
issues.quote: "6 (Extension) | An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims" / "Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics."

issues.description: The abstract states there was "no empirical support" for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect, yet Table 9 reports a significant identifiability × intervention interaction (p = .015). Even if the targeted contrast failed, the abstract should not summarize the factorial results in a way that appears to contradict the reported statistics.
issues.quote: "We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect."

issues.description: The manuscript proposes evaluating replication success by comparing its effect directly to the original effect size, but the replication changed the design, materials, setting, participant pool, and dependent measure. Directly benchmarking the altered study against the original d = 0.48 is therefore not methodologically clean.
issues.quote: "We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84]) obtained from the power analysis..."

issues.description: Important materials and review links are left as placeholders, which prevents readers and reviewers from accessing all planned documents and independently evaluating the workflow.
issues.quote: "Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>" / "Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>"

issues.description: The original study used ordered probit regression for the discrete donation outcome, but the replication explicitly omits that model. Because the donation variable is bounded and integer-valued ($0–$5), dropping the ordinal/discrete model reduces comparability to the original analysis and may poorly match the outcome scale.
issues.quote: "Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation | This test would not be conducted in the replication"
